concept.name: BGP Anycast & Maglev ECMP Consistent Hashing at Global Edge
concept.title: BGP Anycast & Maglev ECMP Consistent Hashing at Global Edge
concept.tagline: Sub-50 ms global PoP routing via BGP Anycast and flow-preserving L4 scaling via Maglev ECMP tables.
concept.purpose: Understand why DNS-based Geo-routing suffers from stale resolver caches, how BGP Anycast routes packets to the nearest PoP at L3, and how Maglev consistent hashing prevents ECMP reshuffling from resetting active TCP connections.

prerequisites.title: TCP 5-Tuple & Connection State
prerequisites.summary: Know that TCP identifies a connection by (src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port, proto) and resets with RST if packets suddenly land on a different L4/L7 proxy without shared state.

prerequisites.title: Consistent Hashing
prerequisites.summary: Understand how consistent hashing minimizes key movement when backend nodes are added or removed.

spark.summary: BGP Anycast announces the same /24 IP prefix from every global PoP for automatic L3 proximity and DDoS absorption, while Maglev ECMP consistent lookup tables keep 5-tuple TCP flows pinned during L4/L7 scale-out.
spark.keyTakeaway: When routing global user traffic across edge PoPs without stale DNS caches or broken TCP connections, announce a shared IP prefix via BGP Anycast and pair ECMP routers with Maglev consistent-lookup tables plus connection tracking.
spark.byteSummary:
GeoDNS tries to send users to the nearest data center by returning regional IP addresses, but ISP resolvers ignore short TTLs and cache stale IPs for hours—sending traffic to overloaded or dead PoPs. BGP Anycast solves this at Layer 3: every PoP announces the exact same IP prefix (e.g., 198.51.100.0/24) over BGP, and internet routers automatically forward each packet to the topologically closest healthy PoP.

Inside a PoP, traffic arrives at Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) switches that spread packets across N software L4 load balancers. With naive `hash(5-tuple) % N`, adding or removing a single L4 balancer remaps ~90% of active TCP flows to new machines that lack their connection state—triggering a storm of TCP RSTs.

Google's Maglev hashing fixes ECMP reshuffling with a prime-sized lookup table (e.g., M = 65,537 slots) filled by round-robin preference permutations across backends. Lookup is a single O(1) array read (`table[hash(5-tuple) % M]`), while adding or removing a backend only perturbs ~1/N of slots—and pairing it with a local connection-tracking table keeps existing flows pinned while new flows rebalance smoothly.

learningJourney.title: P · Problem & Why Modulo ECMP Breaks Active TCP
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Shows why naive `hash(5-tuple) % N` triggers mass TCP resets during autoscaling or node failure.

explanation.foundation: Suppose a PoP runs N = 10 L4 load balancers behind an ECMP router. Every incoming packet is hashed by its 5-tuple and sent to `hash % 10`.
explanation.core: If LB #3 crashes or you scale up to N = 11, `hash % 11` changes the destination for roughly 10/11 (~91%) of all active TCP connections! Packets for an established connection land on a brand-new L4/L7 box that has never seen its SYN handshake, causing immediate TCP RSTs and dropped user requests.
explanation.deepDive: The same fragility hits at the global layer with GeoDNS: if a PoP goes down, stale ISP DNS caches keep sending traffic to the dead IP for 5–60 minutes, whereas BGP Anycast withdraws the route in seconds across peering routers.

learningJourney.title: R · Representation: BGP Anycast + Maglev Permutation Table
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Explains how L3 Anycast and L4 Maglev tables compose cleanly without centralized state.

explanation.foundation: At the global layer, 30+ PoPs announce the exact same `/24` IPv4 prefix (the minimum routable BGP prefix on the public internet). Each user's ISP picks the shortest BGP AS-path.
explanation.core: Inside each PoP, Maglev builds a lookup table `entry[0..M-1]` where M is a prime much larger than N (e.g., M = 65,537). Each backend `i` generates a pseudo-random permutation of `0..M-1` using two independent hashes `(offset_i, skip_i)`. Backends take turns claiming their next unclaimed slot in `entry[]` until all M slots are filled.
explanation.deepDive: Because every backend claims slots in round-robin turns, load distribution is near-uniform (within <1% variance), unlike classic consistent hashing rings without hundreds of virtual nodes. And packet forwarding requires just one array index—easily running at 10+ Mpps per core in XDP/eBPF.

learningJourney.title: I · Invariant: Deterministic Maglev Table & Conntrack
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Shows the exact Maglev table-fill algorithm and why a local conntrack cache protects the remaining ~1/N flows.

explanation.foundation: Maglev guarantees that if backend `k` is removed, ~`1/N` of the 65,537 slots change, and all other `(N-1)/N` slots keep pointing to the exact same backend.
explanation.core: Every L4 balancer runs the identical deterministic algorithm to build the same 65,537-entry table from the healthy backend list. For existing TCP flows that happen to land in the `1/N` remapped slots during a scale-up, a local LRU connection-tracking table (keyed by 5-tuple) remembers the original L7 backend for established flows.
explanation.deepDive: If a packet misses the local conntrack table (e.g., ECMP shifted it to a sibling L4 node), the L4 balancer can either check a lightweight distributed/GRE forwarder or only apply Maglev to SYN packets while forwarding non-SYN packets via conntrack.

codeExample.title: Maglev Lookup Table Builder (O(M log M) Setup, O(1) Packet Lookup)
codeExample.code:
def build_maglev_table(backends, M=65537):
    n = len(backends)
    if n == 0:
        return []
    perm = []
    for b in backends:
        offset = hash((b, 1)) % M
        skip = (hash((b, 2)) % (M - 1)) + 1
        perm.append((offset, skip))
    next_idx = [0] * n
    entry = [-1] * M
    filled = 0
    while filled < M:
        for i in range(n):
            c = (perm[i][0] + next_idx[i] * perm[i][1]) % M
            while entry[c] >= 0:
                next_idx[i] += 1
                c = (perm[i][0] + next_idx[i] * perm[i][1]) % M
            entry[c] = backends[i]
            next_idx[i] += 1
            filled += 1
            if filled == M:
                break
    return entry

learningJourney.title: M · Mechanics at Scale: BGP Route Shifts & Asymmetric Paths
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Explains why BGP Anycast + stateful TCP can break during internet routing flaps and how to mitigate it.

explanation.foundation: BGP is stateless: an internet router can switch a user's path from PoP A to PoP B mid-download if a peering link flaps.
explanation.core: When a TCP packet arrives at PoP B for a connection initiated at PoP A, PoP B has no TCP state! Two production patterns solve this: (1) QUIC with Connection IDs encoding the home PoP/server ID so PoP B forwards packets over an internal backbone tunnel to PoP A; (2) Anycast-over-tunnel where edge PoPs proxy TCP via a regional origin shield.
explanation.deepDive: During planned PoP maintenance, never kill BGP abruptly: first stop announcing new routes or prepend AS-path (`graceful-shutdown` BGP community `65535:0`), drain active connections for 30–60s, and only then withdraw the `/24` prefix.

decisionFramework.problem: How to route global traffic to the nearest healthy PoP without stale DNS caches or broken TCP state.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use GeoDNS with 60s TTL and modulo ECMP inside each PoP.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: ISP resolvers ignore short TTLs during outages, and modulo ECMP resets ~91% of flows when scaling backends.
decisionFramework.alternatives: GeoDNS + stateful NAT vs. BGP Anycast + Maglev ECMP + DSR.
decisionFramework.decision: Announce shared `/24` via BGP Anycast, run Maglev ECMP + conntrack at L4, and use QUIC CIDs or internal tunnels for PoP-flap resilience.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Requires own ASN and `/24` IPv4 block plus BGP peering, and careful graceful-drain tooling for stateful TCP.

learningJourney.title: E · Edge Cases, Assumptions & When NOT to Use Anycast
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Clarifies `/24` BGP minimums, stateful long-lived streams, and DDoS absorption limits.

explanation.foundation: You cannot announce a single `/32` IP over public BGP—global DFZ routers filter anything more specific than `/24` IPv4 (or `/48` IPv6).
explanation.core: When NOT to use BGP Anycast directly: for multi-hour stateful WebSocket or SSH sessions where mid-stream BGP convergence could shift PoPs, terminate TCP at a stable unicast or QUIC-CID-routed edge, or tunnel straggler packets over a private backbone.
explanation.deepDive: Assumptions & Limitations: Assumes control over an Autonomous System Number (ASN) and >=`/24` IPv4 / `/48` IPv6 space, plus symmetric L4 Maglev backend lists synchronized via health checks. Glossary: BGP Anycast (multiple PoPs announcing the same IP prefix), ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path router hashing), Maglev (prime-sized consistent lookup table), DSR (Direct Server Return bypassing L4 on egress).

decisionExercise.prompt: You scale your PoP's L4 load balancer pool from 8 to 9 nodes using stateless `hash(5-tuple) % N` ECMP. Immediately, 88% of active HTTPS downloads fail with `Connection reset by peer`. What fixes this?

options.label: Lower the DNS TTL from 300s to 5s.
options.explanation: DNS TTLs control which PoP IP a client resolves, not intra-PoP ECMP hashing.

options.label: Replace modulo hashing with a Maglev consistent-lookup table + local conntrack so only ~1/N new flows shift and active flows stay pinned.
options.explanation: Correct! Maglev limits slot churn to ~1/N, and conntrack pins established TCP flows to their original L7 proxy.

options.label: Announce a `/32` IP per load balancer over public BGP.
options.explanation: Public BGP filters prefixes smaller than `/24`.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does Maglev use a prime table size M (e.g., 65,537) much larger than the backend count N?

options.text: Because prime M guarantees every `(offset + j * skip) % M` permutation visits all M slots, and large M keeps load imbalance under 1%.
options.feedback: Correct! Coprime `skip` with prime M visits every slot once, and M >> N smooths rounding differences.

options.text: Because BGP packets are exactly 65,537 bytes long.
options.feedback: Ethernet MTU is 1,500 bytes; 65,537 is a prime table size.

options.text: To force every packet to traverse all N backends.
options.feedback: Each packet is forwarded to exactly one backend.
Maglev indexes the table using `hash(5-tuple) % M`.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Prime M ensures full-period permutations for any `1 <= skip < M`, giving uniform O(1) consistent hashing.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens if you scale an L4 pool behind ECMP using `hash(5-tuple) % N` without Maglev or conntrack?

options.text: Only 1/N of active TCP connections are affected.
options.feedback: Modulo hashing remaps nearly all flows (~(N-1)/N), not 1/N.

options.text: Roughly (N-1)/N of active TCP flows land on a different backend and immediately fail with TCP RSTs.
options.feedback: Correct! Changing the modulus N shifts ~90%+ of hash outputs.

options.text: BGP automatically buffers all TCP packets until scale-out finishes.
options.feedback: BGP is stateless L3 routing and never buffers TCP streams.
TCP resets fail the connection unless the app retries.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Modulo hashing is catastrophic for stateful L4 pools; consistent hashing (Maglev) + conntrack is required.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is `/24` the minimum IPv4 prefix typically announced over public BGP Anycast?

options.text: Global BGP peering routers filter prefixes longer than `/24` (more specific than 256 IPs) to prevent routing table explosion.
options.feedback: Correct! Announcing a `/25` or `/32` gets dropped by Tier-1 ISPs.

options.text: IPv4 headers only have 24 bits for addresses.

options.feedback: `/24` is a BGP prefix mask length, not a header size.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Public DFZ BGP policies drop IPv4 prefixes smaller than `/24` (and IPv6 smaller than `/48`).

beginner.summary: BGP Anycast routes users to the nearest data center automatically, while Maglev keeps TCP connections from breaking when servers are added or removed.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When serving global traffic across multiple PoPs, use BGP Anycast for fast routing and Maglev consistent hashing so scaling servers does not drop active connections.
beginner.byteSummary: With BGP Anycast, every global location shares the same IP so the internet routes users to the closest one. Inside each location, Maglev uses a shared lookup table so adding a server doesn't reset everyone's TCP connection.

intermediate.summary: Combine BGP Anycast `/24` announcements for L3 proximity with Maglev's 65,537-slot ECMP table and local conntrack to keep TCP flows intact at scale.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When building a global edge ingress, pair BGP Anycast with Maglev consistent hashing and local conntrack so scale-out only shifts ~1/N new flows.
intermediate.byteSummary: BGP Anycast eliminates stale GeoDNS caches at L3, while Maglev's prime-sized permutation table + 5-tuple conntrack limits flow disruption to ~1/N new connections during L4/L7 pool changes.

advanced.summary: Global BGP Anycast with graceful-shutdown communities, XDP Maglev ECMP + DSR, and QUIC CID / backbone tunneling for mid-stream BGP convergence.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When operating stateful connections behind global BGP Anycast, pair XDP Maglev + DSR with graceful BGP drain and QUIC Connection IDs to survive internet route flaps.
advanced.byteSummary: Running Maglev + conntrack in eBPF/XDP with Direct Server Return scales L4 ingress to 10+ Mpps/core, while QUIC CIDs and BGP `graceful-shutdown` communities prevent mid-stream resets during PoP maintenance or BGP flaps.
